cards.front: Recall a key point about The Electoral System & Voting
cards.back: First Past the Post (FPTP): used for UK general elections. The country is divided into 650 constituencies; each elects one MP by simple plurality (most votes wins). Strengths: simple to understand, produces strong majority governments, clear MP-constituency link. Weaknesses: disproportional (winning party often gets a majority of seats with less than 50% of votes), wasted votes in safe seats, smaller parties under-represented.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The Electoral System & Voting
cards.back: Proportional representation (PR): party seats match their vote share. Used in many European countries. The Additional Member System (AMS) is used for Scottish Parliament and Welsh Senedd elections. The Single Transferable Vote (STV) is used in Northern Ireland. PR is fairer but often produces coalition governments.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The Electoral System & Voting
cards.back: The franchise (right to vote): expanded over centuries: 1832 (property-owning men), 1867 (urban working men), 1918 (all men over 21, women over 30), 1928 (equal suffrage at 21), 1969 (voting age reduced to 18), 2015 (16 for Scottish independence referendum). Debates: should the voting age be lowered to 16 for all UK elections?

cards.front: Recall a key point about The Electoral System & Voting
cards.back: Types of elections: general elections (MPs, FPTP), devolved elections (MSPs/MSs/MLAs, AMS/STV), local elections (councillors, FPTP), European elections (closed list PR, now irrelevant post-Brexit), Police and Crime Commissioner elections (supplementary vote), and by-elections.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The Electoral System & Voting
cards.back: Electoral reform: the 2011 AV referendum was rejected (68% against). Arguments for PR: fairer, more representative, every vote counts. Arguments against: FPTP produces stable governments, PR produces weak coalitions, and FPTP gives a clear MP-constituency link. The Electoral Reform Society campaigns for PR.

cards.front: What should you know about citizenship studies exam tips — the electoral system & voting?
cards.back: 1. For The Electoral System & Voting questions, use citizenship terminology and reference democratic processes accurately 2. Consider multiple viewpoints — including those you disagree with 3. Link The Electoral System & Voting to current affairs and real-world examples where possible 4. When evaluating, consider both rights and responsibilities 5. Structure longer answers: identify the issue, analyse different perspectives, reach a justified view
Evaluate whether the UK should replace First Past the Post with proportional representation for general elections.

cards.front: Understanding The Electoral System & Voting in British Context
cards.back: The Electoral System & Voting is a core topic in GCSE Citizenship Studies that requires understanding of how the UK political and legal systems work, and how citizens can participate effectively. The specification requires you to know how British democracy functions, understand your rights and responsibilities as a citizen, and be able to take informed and responsible action on citizenship issues.

cards.front: The Electoral System & Voting and UK Democratic Processes
cards.back: The UK is a parliamentary democracy where citizens exercise power through elected representatives. Understanding the electoral system & voting requires knowledge of how democratic processes work: general elections (first past the post), devolved elections (additional member system for Scotland and Wales), local elections, and referendums. cards.front: Rights, Responsibilities and The Electoral System & Voting
cards.back: UK citizens have both rights and responsibilities. Key rights include: the right to vote, freedom of speech, freedom of religion, the right to a fair trial, and the right to privacy. These rights are protected by the Human Rights Act 1998, which incorporates the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law.
